newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - Worst is over for French banks - bank association.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Worst is over for French banks - bank association.

text.p: Prospects for French commercial banks, long dogged by poor profits and an uneven competitive playing field, appear to be improving at last, says Michel Freyche, chairman of the Association of French Banks.

After several years of sounding the alarm about the health of French banks, the AFB, which represents the country's 430 commercial banks, says it sees grounds for optimism about the sector in some of the banks' half-year results.
Much stronger earnings from financial market activities, cost-cutting and a stabilisation of provisions which had devastated banks' balance sheets have all played a role in improving the picture.
"We reached bottom," Freyche said. "There has been a clear improvement in the results compared with last year."
Among those banks which surprised analysts with better than expected results were two of France's biggest commercial banks.
Banque Nationale de Paris (BNP) reported an 80 percent jump in first half profits to 1.74 billion francs. And Societe Generale announced a 21 percent rise in profit to 2.73 billion francs.
Domestically, French banks still face problems of weak credit demand, due to a sluggish economy, and margins that are among the lowest in the world as a result of fierce competition.
"But there have been excellent performances by international banking activities and a stabilising of provisions," Freyche said.

For several years, the balance sheets of some of France's biggest banks were hammered by charges to cover exposure to a collapse in mid-1990 of the property market that hit at the same as the the economy went into a downturn.
The loans to the property sector alone cost banks more than 150 billion French francs ($28.96 billion) in writeoffs over the past six years.

Freyche is optimistic the banks could soon be delivering an average return on equity of 10 to 15 percent compared to the current five to six percent, stripping out Credit Lyonnais, the state-owned banking group which racked up huge losses as a result of an expansion binge in the 1980s. "A return on equity of 10 to 15 percent should be rapidly attained," he said.

But to improve the outlook for traditional retail banking activities, the AFB says two things are needed -- better loan demand which hinges on the economy picking up and an end to what it says is cut-throat competition from mutual and savings banks.
Freyche hopes that the group may finally make headway in its crusade to end competitive distortions in the banking market which it says threaten the long-term viability of the sector.
"We could see progress within a reasonable period of time," he said. "I don't think anyone now disputes the validity of our arguments in favour of a truly competitive financial landscape."
He said the group had made the government aware of the problems and the AFB was confident that a parliamentary commission report due at the end of the year will pave the way for changes.
"We think that this report will contain all the elements to justify the need at last to act," he said.

The commercial banks have long complained about what they say is unfair competition from non-commercial banks -- the mutual banks, the post office, the Caisse d'Epargne savings bank network and other specialist financial institutions which control more than 40 percent of the French market.

These institutions, they note, do not share the commercial banks' need to generate profits to achieve rates of return on capital required by shareholders. They also enjoy special privileges such as longer opening hours and savings products which have helped them win market share.
So far, the AFB has seen a few changes -- the government has opened up the market for subsidised housing loans to all banks.
But "on most important issues, there has been no progress and that's pity. We're going to have a single European market and we don't even have a single banking market," Freyche said.
Still, the AFB has powerful allies in seeking change. Jean-Claude Trichet, governor of the Bank of France, has called for "an end to competitive distortion".

Also driving change, the AFB says, will be European monetary and economic union set to start on January 1, 1999. The AFB believes the government needs to ensure a healthy banking sector that can hold its own in a unified Europe.
($1=5.179 French Franc)
